Exercise is a broad topic, so here's a general orientation to how different movements fit together, along with a few entries from the list you shared.

One useful way to think about training is by movement pattern rather than by muscle name.

Squat patterns. Goblet squat and bodyweight squat both train a squat pattern. The goblet version adds load and tends to help people learn to stay upright, since the weight sits in front of the chest. Bodyweight squats are easier to scale by changing tempo or depth.

Hinge and posterior chain. Back extension is a simple hinge-adjacent movement that works the spinal erectors, glutes and hamstrings through a controlled range. It pairs well with calf work like bodyweight calf raise or barbell calf raise, since both are often trained with higher repetitions.

Pressing and pushing. Barbell bench press is the loaded horizontal press. Its bodyweight relatives include archer push ups and pseudo planche push ups, which shift more demand onto one arm or toward the shoulders. Machine assisted dips sit in between, allowing a dip pattern with adjustable assistance.

Pulling. Assisted pull ups and band assisted pull ups are the two common ways to reduce load in a pull up. Archer pull ups and archer pull ups on a bar reduce assistance further by emphasising one side. Band pull apart is a light horizontal pull that many people use as a warm up for the upper back and rear shoulders.

Core and anti-extension. Plank, high plank, bear plank hold, reverse plank, and ring plank all resist movement rather than create it. Reverse plank biases the posterior chain and glutes. Plank knee tuck and Pilates leg pull front add a moving limb, which raises the coordination demand.

Mobility and stretching. The banded stretches in the list, such as banded ankle stretch, banded lat stretch, banded chest stretch and banded figure-4 stretch, are generally held for time and used to explore range rather than to build strength.

Conditioning. Walking, stationary bike and air bike are duration-and-distance options. Battle rope double slam and burpees are higher-intensity intervals that also involve the upper body and full-body coordination.

Hand and forearm work. Wrist curls appear with several implements: dumbbell, barbell, cable, EZ-bar and kettlebell. Reverse wrist curls train the opposite direction and are often included alongside them.

A few practical notes. Aim for controlled range of motion and stop any movement that produces discomfort rather than pushing through it. Skill-based holds like planche and back lever take a long time to develop and are usually approached progressively. Each session follows the same shape: a short easy warm-up, a cardio block, a strength circuit, then a calm cool-down. The cardio is steady walking or marching in place, which is joint-friendly at home and easy to scale by pace or time. For fat loss, consistency across the week matters more than any single hard session, and strength work helps you keep muscle while you lose fat.

- Warm-up: walking or marching in place, 5 minutes, easy pace

  - Bodyweight calf raise, 15 reps

  - Bear crawl, 6 to 8 steps forward and back
  - Bicycle crunch, 10 per side
- Cool-down: slow walking and easy stretches, 5 minutes

- Circuit, 2 rounds
  - Bodyweight reverse lunge, 10 per leg
  - Plank, 25 to 35 seconds
  - Bench leg pull-in, 10 to 12 reps
  - Self-resisted row, 12 reps
  - Bodyweight squat, 10 reps
- Cool-down: slow walking and easy stretches, 5 minutes

How to progress

Add a few reps, a few seconds, or slightly more cardio time each week when the previous week felt manageable. Keep at least one easy day between sessions where you can.

messages.content: Explain the bodyweight squat movement

results.outputText:
The bodyweight squat is a foundational lower-body movement that uses only your own weight. You stand with feet roughly shoulder-width apart, toes slightly out, then bend at the hips and knees to lower your body as if sitting down toward a chair. The goal is to keep your chest tall, your spine neutral, and your knees tracking in the same direction as your toes. You descend to a depth you can control while keeping your heels grounded, then push through your feet to stand back up.

A few points that tend to matter:
- Depth is individual. Go only as far as you can while maintaining a neutral spine and stable knees. A partial range done with control is valid.
- Breathing is usually inhale on the way down, exhale on the way up.
- If you feel discomfort in your knees, hips, or back, stop the movement and consider having it assessed rather than pushing through it.
- Progressions can include a box or chair to sit back to, or a slower tempo, before adding reps or load.

This is general movement information, not a personal program.
